thread.title: In my last article we explored the notion that the DRAM prod

author: William Tidwell
title: In my last article we explored the notion that the DRAM prod
text:
In my last article we explored the notion that the DRAM producers are likely to be deterred from being aggressive building additional wafer capacity in the face of the prospect of the (relatively) near-term arrival of new, non-volatile memories that will initially augment, and over time, replace DRAM. We cited IMFT’s announcement that they completed an expansion of the Lehi 3D XPoint fab in November of last year as a clear signal of the confidence of Intel ( INTC ) and Micron ( MU ) that the new technology was on track for commercial success. We then went on to speculate about the potential for Apple ( AAPL ) to be an early adopter of this technology.
As it happens, other folks are thinking about that possibility as well. Recently, Alan Neibel of Webfeet Research presented just this scenario at SNIA’s recent “Persistent Memory Summit.” It seems that Mr. Neibel has a theory about the future of the memory industry, and it’s one that has some tantalizing elements in it for Apple and IM that are worth teasing out. Let’s consider what Mr. Neibel has to say.
The Neibel gambit, if we may call it that, begins with a supposition about a revolutionary new memory, called “Non-Volatile RAM” (NVRAM for short) that's close at hand. He outlines its characteristics and capabilities in this slide:

This slide is notable for a number of reasons, but probably most of all because it defines, in the combination of its features, a nearly perfect memory. Its power consumption should be excellent because it’s persistent, and that means that, unlike DRAM, it does not need to be refreshed. It has decent endurance (100’s of billions of cycles) and DRAM-like latency. It's also DRAM-like in that it is, unlike many NVMs, DDR4 compatible. So what is this new memory? Mr. Neibel is coy on this point. Let’s compare it against the memory taxonomy generously provided in the Handy/Coughlin presentation that preceded Neibel’s talk. Take a look at the chart below. Do you see a fit?

The comparison isn’t straightforward because the slide doesn’t match the taxonomy categories. It’s clearly not PCM – it’s faster and has much greater endurance. It doesn’t fit FeRAM well either. Is it a form of ReRAM? If so, it has much greater endurance and way higher density than the highest density shipping ReRAM die from Panasonic – a 4Mb product. The closest memory that would be a fit would be MRAM, but here we run into the same issue as ReRAM – density. Note the one bullet-point of the Neibel slide that I have not mentioned, the “Higher Density Roadmaps, 8 – 32 layers.” This implies a memory density that's potentially NAND like, which at scale-out production levels would mean that this mystery memory could be much less costly than DRAM. This is light years away from current MRAM memories. Everspin Corporation just began delivering 256Mb dies in small volumes, for example. Contrast this density with currently generations of DRAM at 8Gb and NAND at 256 to 512Gb per die.
Unless something truly miraculous has happened in some R&D lab somewhere recently, neither ReRAM or MRAM is ready for primetime now – nor will they be any time before well into the next decade. Oh, did I say that Niebel’s forecast includes commercial delivery of the new wonder chip in late 2019? Here’s his market synopsis slide:

Before pursuing this further let’s address the elephant in the room. Could Niebel’s mystery memory be the “New Memory” that Micron has been talking about for several years now? Let’s compare Neibel’s positioning against Micron’s as depicted in the following slide from last year’s Analyst Conference.

Admittedly, we have only two touch points from Micron that intersect Neibel’s criteria, so we have relatively little to go on and certainly nothing conclusive. Considering only the “cost/bit” dimension for the moment, Scott DeBoer (Micron’s technology chief and author of the slide) would have to have positioned the New Memory well to the left, much closer to NAND (and directly over 3D XPoint) if it were to fit Neibel’s mystery NVRAM. On the other hand, the “performance/speed” metric fits DeBoer’s New Memory positioning very well – not equal to DRAM, but very close.
Is there any possible explanation for the discontinuities and discrepancies that we have identified above? Well, yes, there’s this thing called time – calendar time – that could bring the memory cost attribute into closer congruence. Remember now that DRAM and NAND cost and density are a moving target – both are advancing. Let’s assume that Neibel’s memory is delivered to market at the end of 2019 as an 8-layer die to be compared to the then current “1Y” (15/16nm) DRAM and a 128 layer Gen 4 NAND. At 8 layers, the presumed density of the Neibel memory would indicate a positioning on DeBoer’s chart that would be much closer to NAND than DRAM, right?
So where are we with this? Niebel’s revolutionary new NVM is in the ballpark with the Micron positioning chart, but we’re guessing. For now let’s assume it does and see where that leads us as we analyze Neibel’s “Market Synopsis” slide above.
As we’ll soon see, Neibel has very clear ideas about how this new memory would come to market. He questions whether it would be “price competitive” with XP. Let’s take a moment and tease that out. In pursuit of that objective let’s take a leap and assume that Gen 2 XP is shipping in this same late 2020 time frame and that it will be a 4-layer, 512Gb die. What would something like that cost to make? Using the admittedly sparse data available to the public I have constructed a model that's giving me $.74/GB as a cost (assuming 40k wpm at 60% yields) of the Gen 1 128Gb chip. (For context, Intel’s Optane 900P SSD is selling for roughly $1.25/GB, so maybe the model’s cost estimate isn’t too far off.) If we now take a further assumptive leap and assume that Gen 2 XP will be a 4 layer, 512 Gb die and bump monthly wafer output over 2019 and 2020 to 90k wpm and yields to 80%, that would get us to a $.38/GB for Gen 2 XP cost in the Gen 2 ramp year of 2019 and $.18/GB for the full year of 2020.
The chart below shows how that compares to current and contemporaneous memories in Q4 of 2020.

How would that compare to Neibel’s “NVRAM?” Once again, we’re only guessing but IF it’s an MRAM of some type then the cell size is roughly a factor of 3 bigger than XP (a PCM memory) which implies that each layer of Neibel’s NVRAM would be roughly one-third as dense as a corresponding XP layer (at the same lithography), so if I have double the layers then theoretically the new memory will be in the ballpark but not quite as cheap as XP. If we model that at the fab volumes and yields we have projected for XP, then the 2021 cost of NVRAM could be roughly $.18
So, OK, close enough in cost to be competitive with XP. It’s the last bullet point in Neibel’s “NVRAM competitive positioning” topic, however, that must give us some pause. The one that says, “Secondary supply suggests an open standard.” Hmm…
What “open standard?” If there's one thing that we can count on for sure it is that the IP that backs this wonder memory is as proprietary as proprietary can get. By the time this new memory is commercialized the supplier that produces it will have incurred tens, if not hundreds of millions in R&D cost that must be recovered. And the only way that happens is to have large-scale production of a highly scalable memory design, with high gross margins rewarding the first mover/movers. Collaboration with another supplier? Possibly. “Open standard?” Over time - quite possibly, but fresh out of the box – no way!
Not that having a second source for this new technology is not important. This is a legitimate issue that must be addressed. And there are some very good reasons for having a second, independent source of what we may presume is a highly desirable product differentiator for the OEM’s that adopt it. Would it work if one supplier produced the memory in two different fabs? Good question. We are in uncharted waters here. We have NAND as a potential analog, but (industry veterans correct me if I’m wrong) the driving application for NAND was the consumer-dominated market of film replacement – hardly a mission critical application. Would Apple, other mobile OEMS, and the Hyper Cloud data centers commit to anything more than a niche offering involving XP until there was a credible second source? IM is about to test this old school orthodoxy with their Optane and QuantX franchises because, as of this date, there's no fab other than the recently expanded Lehi complex that's making 3D XPoint. Could any major customer make a significant product line commitment to a single-fab supplier? We’re about to find out.
The reason we are spending some time ruminating on this sourcing issue will become apparent as we consider the last bullet-point in Neibel’s slide. Here he identifies his theory of how this new memory builds manufacturing scale and comes to market. So it’s the mobile market that he identifies as the initial adopter – for replacing both “DRAM and NAND.” We get a better view of how he expects this to happen in his next slide.

Apple almost $3B in 2022. In the bottom half of the chart we see what looks like a forecast for various types of NVDIMM sales and, as a part of that, a forecast for XP NVDIMM sales rising from (presumably) $171m in 2018 to $4.3B in 2021, only to subside to $3.1B in 2022 as NVRAM displaces it. Is that in the mobile market or the whole market? We don’t know. (The chart is frankly incomprehensible and the presentation at the recent SNIA Persistent Memory Summit does nothing to clear it up.)
So what are we to conclude from all this?
For me, the main takeaway is larger than any conclusions we might draw from Neibel’s presentation. The overarching point is that the industry is starting to prepare for the rise of NVM. Serious, experienced industry analysts are creating frameworks for the analysis of the impact of Non-Volatile Memory. Obviously we are still at a very early stage, but this train is leaving the station. The commercialization of 3D XPoint NVDIMMS will open an era of rapid and fundamental change in the memory industry and in the broader technical ecosystem.
Where does Apple really fit in all this? I've got to think that where there is smoke there is fire. Apple may or may not be an early adopter of NVDIMM but for my money it makes sense that it would be interested, assuming of course that the performance and price of the persistent memory on offer would meet their needs. Initially there won't be nearly enough production to meet all of Apple's requirements, but that wouldn't rule out Apple launching a leading edge phone into a relatively small (and likely very pricey) niche. 
Hopefully we’ll hear a lot more about Micron’s plans for XP and “New Memory” in the May Analyst conference. Before we close, let’s explore the implications of the only real projection we have ever received from Micron regarding the sale of XP – in this case for the server market.

As you can see, this slide dates from early 2016, so it reflects Micron’s early thinking on market development. The slide projects about 1.5EB of XP sales into the server market in 2020, doubling to almost 3EB in 2021. 16% of servers were projected to employ the memory, climbing to 22% in 2021 and 27% in 2022. Given the year over year bit growth, content is obviously being projected to grow even faster than server penetration.
Is there anything about this slide that we should keep in mind as we consider the comments they will make in May? Maybe just this – if my model and underlying assumptions are anywhere near close, Micron’s projection of 1.5 EB of server sales equates to roughly $1B of XP revenue in this market in 2020. That sounds like a very modest goal to me. Of course there’s a lot of market territory that this slide doesn’t cover – most notably the mobile and client businesses, both of which could be bigger. Be that as it may, two years is a lot of time. Will the Micron of 2018 deliver a more bullish message at the upcoming May presentation? I’m going to be listening carefully to find out.
